questions.question: The angle of attack of an aerofoil is defined as the angle:-

options.text: between the chord line and the relative airflow
between the chord line and the horizontal
between the blade pitch angle and the rotor disc plane
between the leading edge and the trailing edge

questions.explanation: The angle of attack is the angle between the chord line of the aerofoil and the direction of the relative airflow (RAF). It is not the same as the pitch angle, which is measured relative to the rotor disc plane.

questions.question: As the angle of attack of an aerofoil is increased, the centre of pressure will:-

options.text: move forward
move rearward
remain stationary
move forward then rearward at the stall

questions.explanation: As angle of attack increases (up to the stalling angle), the centre of pressure moves forward along the chord line. At the stall, the CP moves rapidly rearward as the lift distribution changes dramatically.

questions.question: With reference to the lift formula, if the speed is doubled whilst the angle of attack remains constant, the lift will:-

options.text: be four times greater
be doubled
be halved
remain the same

questions.explanation: Lift = CL × ½ρV² × S. Since lift is proportional to V² (velocity squared), doubling the speed results in 2² = 4 times the lift, assuming all other factors remain constant.

questions.question: A design feature which is used to reduce induced drag is:-

options.text: washout
a symmetrical aerofoil section
increased blade chord
a higher rotor RPM

questions.explanation: Washout (blade twist) reduces the angle of attack progressively towards the blade tip, which reduces the strength of the tip vortices and therefore reduces induced drag. It also helps distribute lift more evenly along the blade span.

questions.question: Washout is incorporated in some blade designs in order to:-

options.text: reduce induced drag
increase the stalling speed
reduce profile drag
increase the blade pitch angle at the tip

questions.explanation: Washout (blade twist) progressively reduces the pitch angle from root to tip. This reduces the angle of attack at the tips, weakening tip vortices and reducing induced drag. It also helps prevent tip stalling and provides a more even lift distribution.

questions.question: The effect of blow-back (flap-back) is to:-

options.text: reduce the helicopter's forward speed
increase the helicopter's forward speed
cause the helicopter to yaw
increase the coning angle

questions.explanation: Flap-back occurs in forward flight because the advancing blade experiences a higher relative airspeed and flaps up, while the retreating blade flaps down. The net effect tilts the rotor disc aft, which reduces forward speed unless corrected with forward cyclic.

questions.question: The coning angle is determined:-

options.text: by the combined effect of rotor thrust and centrifugal force
solely by the rotor RPM
by the tail rotor thrust
by the weight of the helicopter only

questions.explanation: The coning angle is the result of two opposing forces: rotor thrust (lift) acts upward on each blade causing it to rise, while centrifugal force acts outward tending to keep the blades in the plane of rotation. The balance between these two forces determines the coning angle.

questions.question: In a turn, rotor thrust needs to overcome:-

options.text: the vertical component of weight and provide centripetal force
only the weight of the helicopter
only the centrifugal force
the tail rotor thrust and weight

questions.explanation: In a banked turn, the rotor thrust must be increased to provide two components: a vertical component to support the weight of the helicopter, and a horizontal component to provide the centripetal force needed to turn. This is why more power is needed in a turn.

questions.question: Rotor drag (rotor torque) is that force which acts:-

options.text: in the plane of rotation and opposite to the direction of blade travel
perpendicular to the relative airflow
vertically downward on the rotor disc
along the blade span towards the tip

questions.explanation: Rotor drag (torque) acts in the plane of rotation, opposing the direction of blade travel. It is the aerodynamic drag on the blades that the engine must overcome to maintain rotor RPM. This torque reaction causes the fuselage to want to rotate in the opposite direction to the rotor.

questions.question: When a helicopter, maintaining a constant height above ground whilst hovering, is subjected to translational lift:-

options.text: the collective lever must be lowered to maintain height
the collective lever must be raised to maintain height
no change in collective is required
the cyclic must be moved aft

questions.explanation: Translational lift occurs as the helicopter moves into clean, undisturbed air. The rotor becomes more efficient, producing more lift for the same blade angle. To maintain the same height, the pilot must lower the collective to reduce blade angle and prevent the helicopter from climbing.

questions.question: The correct method of recovering from retreating blade stall is to:-

options.text: lower the collective
raise the collective
apply full forward cyclic
increase rotor RPM by raising the throttle

questions.explanation: Retreating blade stall occurs when the retreating blade's angle of attack exceeds the critical angle. Recovery requires reducing the blade angle of attack by lowering the collective (reducing pitch), reducing airspeed, and reducing the severity of any manoeuvre.

questions.question: Translating tendency in a helicopter with anti-clockwise rotating rotor blades is corrected by:-

options.text: tilting the mast or rotor disc slightly to the left
applying the left anti-torque pedal
applying right cyclic
increasing the tail rotor pitch

questions.explanation: Translating tendency (tail rotor drift) is caused by the tail rotor producing a lateral thrust that pushes the helicopter sideways. In a helicopter with anti-clockwise rotating blades (viewed from above), the tail rotor pushes the aircraft to the right. This is corrected by a built-in left tilt of the mast or rotor disc.

questions.question: When power is applied, a helicopter with an anti-clockwise rotating main rotor will tend to:-

options.text: yaw to the right which must be corrected with the left pedal
yaw to the left which must be corrected with the right pedal
pitch nose up
roll to the left

questions.explanation: Newton's third law: the torque reaction to an anti-clockwise rotating main rotor (viewed from above) causes the fuselage to yaw clockwise (to the right). The pilot must apply left anti-torque pedal to increase tail rotor thrust and counteract this yaw.

questions.question: Lowering the collective lever will:-

options.text: simultaneously decrease the blade angle of all the rotor blades by the same amount
decrease the blade angle of only the advancing blade
increase the blade angle of all rotor blades
have no effect on blade angle

questions.explanation: The collective control changes the pitch angle of all rotor blades simultaneously and by the same amount. Lowering the collective reduces the pitch angle of all blades equally, decreasing total rotor thrust. Raising it increases the pitch of all blades equally.

questions.question: Lead-lagging (dragging) is:-

options.text: the forward or aft movement of a blade in the plane of rotation
the up and down movement of a blade
the twisting of a blade about its span axis
the vibration of the blade at high speed

questions.explanation: Lead-lag (dragging) is the movement of a rotor blade forward or aft in the plane of rotation. It occurs due to conservation of angular momentum — as a blade flaps up, its centre of mass moves closer to the axis of rotation, causing it to lead (speed up). When it flaps down, it lags (slows down). A drag hinge or elastomeric bearing accommodates this movement.

questions.question: Lateral stability in a helicopter refers to stability in the:-

options.text: rolling plane
pitching plane
yawing plane
vertical plane

questions.explanation: Lateral stability is stability about the longitudinal axis, which is the rolling plane. It is the helicopter's tendency to return to a wings-level attitude after being disturbed by a gust or control input that causes a roll.

questions.question: During autorotation:-

options.text: collective is used to control rotor RPM
cyclic is used to control rotor RPM
the throttle is used to control rotor RPM
the anti-torque pedals are used to control rotor RPM

questions.explanation: During autorotation, the engine is no longer driving the rotor. Rotor RPM is maintained by the upward flow of air through the rotor disc. The collective controls the blade pitch angle, which directly affects rotor RPM — raising collective increases drag on the blades and reduces RPM, lowering it reduces drag and increases RPM.

questions.question: If high rotor RPM is experienced during autorotation from high altitude:-

options.text: the collective pitch lever should be raised to reduce it
the collective pitch lever should be lowered
the cyclic should be moved forward
the anti-torque pedals should be applied

questions.explanation: If rotor RPM becomes too high during autorotation, raising the collective increases the blade pitch angle, which increases drag on the blades and reduces rotor RPM. This is the primary method of controlling rotor RPM during autorotation.

questions.question: Directional stability in a helicopter refers to stability in the:-

options.text: yawing plane
rolling plane
pitching plane
vertical plane

questions.explanation: Directional stability is stability about the normal (vertical) axis, which is the yawing plane. It is the helicopter's tendency to maintain or return to its heading after a yaw disturbance. The tail rotor, vertical fin, and fuselage shape all contribute to directional stability.

questions.question: The effect of the driven, or propeller region during autorotation is to:-

options.text: produce rotor drag which opposes the rotor RPM
provide a good rotational force
produce the majority of the lift
have no significant effect on autorotation

questions.explanation: During autorotation, the driven (propeller) region is the outer portion of the blade near the tips. In this region, the total aerodynamic force is tilted behind the axis of rotation, producing a drag component that opposes rotor RPM. The driving region (mid-span) provides the force that maintains RPM.

questions.question: The effect on a helicopter's performance of an increase in humidity is:-

options.text: to decrease the lift
to increase the lift
to have no effect on performance
to increase engine power output

questions.explanation: Humid air is less dense than dry air because water vapour molecules (H₂O, molecular weight 18) replace heavier nitrogen (N₂, molecular weight 28) and oxygen (O₂, molecular weight 32) molecules. Lower air density reduces both rotor lift and engine performance.

questions.question: As the angle of bank during a level turn is increased, additional engine power must be applied in order to:-

options.text: compensate for the increased induced drag because of greater blade angles
counter the increased centrifugal force
maintain tail rotor effectiveness
prevent the rotor RPM from increasing

questions.explanation: In a level turn, the rotor must produce more total thrust to support the weight and provide centripetal force. This requires higher blade angles (more collective), which increases induced drag. Additional engine power is needed to overcome this increased drag and maintain rotor RPM.

questions.question: Rectified airspeed (RAS) or Calibrated airspeed (CAS) is:-

options.text: IAS corrected for instrument and position errors
TAS corrected for instrument and position errors
IAS corrected for density altitude
TAS corrected for compressibility

questions.explanation: Calibrated Airspeed (CAS), also known as Rectified Airspeed (RAS), is the Indicated Airspeed (IAS) corrected for instrument errors (in the ASI itself) and position errors (caused by the location of the pitot tube and static ports on the aircraft).

questions.question: If you need to descend quickly (another aircraft coming toward you), the best method is to:-

options.text: lower the collective, reduce engine power, and move cyclic forward
raise the collective and apply full forward cyclic
enter autorotation immediately
apply full aft cyclic and increase power

questions.explanation: To descend quickly and safely: lower the collective to reduce rotor thrust, reduce engine power, and move the cyclic forward to increase the rate of descent. This combination provides a rapid controlled descent while maintaining rotor RPM and aircraft control.

questions.question: In comparison to a straight climb, during a climbing turn:-

options.text: the rate of climb will reduce
the rate of climb will remain the same
the rate of climb will increase
the airspeed will increase

questions.explanation: During a climbing turn, some of the available rotor thrust is used to provide the centripetal force for the turn. This means less thrust is available for climbing, so the rate of climb reduces compared to a straight climb at the same power setting.

questions.question: During a straight climb at a constant speed:-

options.text: lift is less than weight
lift is greater than weight
lift equals weight
thrust equals drag

questions.explanation: In a steady (constant speed) climb, the flight path is inclined upward. The weight acts vertically downward, but lift acts perpendicular to the flight path (not vertically). A component of thrust supports part of the weight along the flight path, so lift only needs to balance the component of weight perpendicular to the flight path — which is less than the total weight.

questions.question: Dissymmetry of lift is caused by:-

options.text: the difference in relative airspeed between the advancing and retreating blades in forward flight
the difference in blade pitch angle between the advancing and retreating blades
the coning angle of the rotor blades
the tail rotor thrust

questions.explanation: In forward flight, the advancing blade has a relative airspeed of rotational speed plus forward speed, while the retreating blade has rotational speed minus forward speed. This difference in airspeed creates unequal lift — dissymmetry of lift — which is compensated for by blade flapping.

questions.question: The purpose of the flapping hinge on a fully articulated rotor head is to:-

options.text: allow the blades to move up and down to compensate for dissymmetry of lift
allow the blades to change pitch angle
allow the blades to lead and lag
reduce the coning angle

questions.explanation: The flapping hinge allows each blade to move up and down independently. In forward flight, the advancing blade flaps up (reducing its angle of attack and lift) and the retreating blade flaps down (increasing its angle of attack and lift), thereby equalising lift across the disc and compensating for dissymmetry of lift.

questions.question: The feathering hinge (or bearing) on a rotor head allows:-

options.text: each blade to change its pitch angle about its spanwise axis
each blade to flap up and down
each blade to lead and lag in the plane of rotation
the rotor disc to tilt

questions.explanation: The feathering hinge (or feathering bearing) allows each blade to rotate about its spanwise (longitudinal) axis, changing its pitch angle. This is how the pilot's collective and cyclic inputs are transmitted to the blades to control thrust and disc tilt.

questions.question: Ground effect in a helicopter is most effective when hovering at a height of:-

options.text: approximately half the rotor diameter or less above the surface
one full rotor diameter above the surface
two rotor diameters above the surface
any height below 500 ft AGL

questions.explanation: Ground effect is most pronounced when the helicopter is hovering at a skid/wheel height of approximately half the rotor diameter or less. At this height, the ground restricts the downward flow of air, reducing induced drag and the power required to hover. The effect diminishes rapidly above this height.

questions.question: Hovering in ground effect (IGE) compared to hovering out of ground effect (OGE) requires:-

options.text: less power
more power
the same power
less power only at high altitude

questions.explanation: Hovering IGE requires less power than OGE because the ground surface restricts the rotor downwash, reducing the induced velocity and therefore the induced drag. This means the rotor is more efficient and less power is needed to produce the same amount of thrust.

questions.question: Effective translational lift (ETL) typically occurs at an airspeed of approximately:-

options.text: 16 to 24 knots
5 to 10 knots
30 to 40 knots
50 to 60 knots

questions.explanation: Effective Translational Lift (ETL) is noticeable at approximately 16 to 24 knots. At this speed, the rotor moves into relatively undisturbed air, the induced flow is reduced, and the rotor becomes significantly more efficient. The pilot will feel a noticeable vibration and the helicopter will tend to climb.

questions.question: The region of a rotor blade that produces the driving force during autorotation is the:-

options.text: mid-span section (driving region)
blade tip section
blade root section
entire blade equally

questions.explanation: During autorotation, the blade is divided into three regions: the stall region (near the root), the driving region (mid-span), and the driven/propeller region (near the tips). The driving region is where the total aerodynamic force is tilted forward of the axis of rotation, providing the force that maintains rotor RPM.

questions.question: During autorotation, the stall region of the blade is located:-

options.text: near the blade root
at the blade tips
at the mid-span of the blade
evenly distributed along the blade

questions.explanation: The stall region is near the blade root where the rotational velocity is lowest. The angle of attack in this region exceeds the critical angle, causing the airflow to separate. This region produces drag that opposes rotation but contributes little useful lift or driving force.

questions.question: Gyroscopic precession in a rotor system means that:-

options.text: an applied force takes effect approximately 90° later in the direction of rotation
the rotor disc always remains level
the blades resist any change in pitch angle
an applied force takes effect 180° later

questions.explanation: Gyroscopic precession is a property of rotating bodies. When a force is applied to a spinning rotor disc, the effect of that force is felt approximately 90° later in the direction of rotation. This is why cyclic pitch changes are applied 90° before the point where the disc tilt is desired.

questions.question: The cyclic pitch control on a helicopter is used to:-

options.text: tilt the rotor disc in the desired direction of flight
change the pitch of all blades simultaneously
control the rotor RPM
control the yaw of the helicopter

questions.explanation: The cyclic control changes the pitch angle of each blade cyclically — once per revolution — so that the blade pitch varies as it travels around the disc. This causes the disc to tilt in the desired direction, directing the thrust vector and controlling the helicopter's direction of flight.

questions.question: The anti-torque pedals on a helicopter are used to:-

options.text: control the heading by changing the pitch of the tail rotor blades
control the rate of climb
tilt the main rotor disc
change the pitch of the main rotor blades

questions.explanation: The anti-torque pedals change the pitch angle of the tail rotor blades, which varies the amount of thrust the tail rotor produces. This controls the yaw (heading) of the helicopter by balancing or overcoming the torque reaction from the main rotor.

questions.question: The purpose of the tail rotor on a single main rotor helicopter is to:-

options.text: counteract the torque reaction of the main rotor
provide forward thrust
provide additional lift
reduce the coning angle of the main rotor

questions.explanation: The main rotor torque causes the fuselage to rotate in the opposite direction to the rotor. The tail rotor produces a lateral thrust that counteracts this torque reaction, maintaining directional control. The pilot adjusts tail rotor thrust via the anti-torque pedals.

questions.question: Vortex ring state (settling with power) is most likely to occur when:-

options.text: descending vertically or near-vertically at low airspeed with power applied
climbing at high airspeed
hovering in ground effect
in fast forward flight at cruise speed

questions.explanation: Vortex ring state occurs when the helicopter descends into its own downwash. The conditions are: a rate of descent greater than about 300 ft/min, low forward airspeed (below ETL), and power applied. The recirculating air through the rotor disc causes a loss of effective lift and an increasing rate of descent.

questions.question: The recommended recovery from vortex ring state is to:-

options.text: lower the collective and move the cyclic forward to gain airspeed
raise the collective to maximum power
apply full aft cyclic
enter autorotation and maintain zero airspeed

questions.explanation: Recovery from vortex ring state requires moving the rotor disc into clean, undisturbed air. The standard recovery is to lower the collective to reduce power demand and move the cyclic forward to gain forward airspeed. Once airspeed increases above ETL, the rotor moves into clean air and normal flight can be resumed.

questions.question: Longitudinal stability in a helicopter refers to stability in the:-

options.text: pitching plane
rolling plane
yawing plane
vertical plane

questions.explanation: Longitudinal stability is stability about the lateral axis, which is the pitching plane. It is the helicopter's tendency to return to its trimmed pitch attitude after a disturbance. The position of the CG relative to the main rotor mast is a key factor in longitudinal stability.

questions.question: A helicopter with its centre of gravity forward of the allowable range will tend to:-

options.text: be nose heavy and may not be able to flare for landing
be tail heavy and difficult to control in forward flight
have no noticeable effect on handling
yaw uncontrollably to the right

questions.explanation: A forward CG makes the helicopter nose heavy. The pilot must apply aft cyclic to compensate, reducing the available cyclic range. In extreme cases, there may not be enough aft cyclic available to flare for landing, which is extremely dangerous.

questions.question: A helicopter with its centre of gravity aft of the allowable range will tend to:-

options.text: be tail heavy and may become uncontrollable in flight
be nose heavy and difficult to hover
have improved forward flight performance
have no effect on handling

questions.explanation: An aft CG makes the helicopter tail heavy. The pilot must apply forward cyclic to compensate. In extreme cases, there may not be enough forward cyclic to maintain control, and the helicopter can enter an uncontrollable nose-high attitude. An aft CG is generally more dangerous than a forward CG.

questions.question: The swash plate assembly consists of:-

options.text: a rotating plate connected to the blades and a non-rotating plate connected to the flight controls
two rotating plates both connected to the blades
a single plate that tilts with the cyclic input
a plate connected only to the collective control

questions.explanation: The swash plate has two parts: a stationary (non-rotating) lower plate connected to the flight controls, and a rotating upper plate connected to the rotor blades via pitch links. The lower plate tilts and rises/lowers based on cyclic and collective inputs, and the upper plate transmits these movements to the blades.

questions.question: The critical azimuth position for retreating blade stall is approximately:-

options.text: 270° (the 9 o'clock position)
90° (the 3 o'clock position)
180° (the 6 o'clock position)
360° (the 12 o'clock position)

questions.explanation: The retreating blade has its lowest relative airspeed at the 270° position (9 o'clock), where the blade is moving directly opposite to the direction of flight. At this point, the blade must have the highest angle of attack to produce its share of lift, making it most susceptible to stalling.

questions.question: Factors that increase the likelihood of retreating blade stall include:-

options.text: high forward speed, high gross weight, high density altitude, and turbulence
low forward speed and low gross weight
hovering in ground effect
low density altitude and smooth air

questions.explanation: Retreating blade stall is more likely with: high forward speed (greater difference between advancing and retreating blade speeds), high gross weight (higher blade angles needed), high density altitude (less dense air requires higher angles of attack), steep or abrupt manoeuvres, and turbulence.

questions.question: The phenomenon known as 'transverse flow effect' occurs because:-

options.text: the air flowing through the rear of the rotor disc has a greater induced velocity than at the front
the advancing blade produces more lift than the retreating blade
the tail rotor interferes with the main rotor airflow
the engine exhaust deflects the rotor downwash

questions.explanation: In forward flight, air entering the rear of the rotor disc has been accelerated downward more than air at the front (which is meeting relatively undisturbed air). This difference in induced velocity across the disc causes the rear of the disc to have a lower angle of attack than the front, resulting in a lateral vibration typically felt as the helicopter transitions through ETL.

questions.question: Density altitude increases with:-

options.text: an increase in temperature, altitude, or humidity
a decrease in temperature only
an increase in atmospheric pressure
a decrease in humidity

questions.explanation: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature. It increases with higher temperature (hot air is less dense), higher altitude (less atmospheric pressure), and higher humidity (water vapour is lighter than dry air). All three reduce air density, degrading helicopter performance.

questions.question: The main effect of operating a helicopter at a weight above the maximum allowable is:-

options.text: reduced performance margins and possible structural damage
improved stability due to the lower CG
increased range due to higher momentum
no significant effect if the CG is within limits

questions.explanation: Operating above maximum allowable weight reduces all performance margins: hover ceiling is lower, rate of climb is reduced, range is decreased, and structural limits may be exceeded. The rotor blades must operate at higher angles of attack, closer to the stall, and the airframe may be overstressed.

questions.question: In a semi-rigid (teetering) rotor system, the blades are:-

options.text: rigidly attached to each other and flap as a unit about a central hinge
independently hinged with separate flapping, feathering, and drag hinges
rigidly attached to the mast with no hinges
free to move independently in all three axes

questions.explanation: In a semi-rigid (teetering) rotor system, the two blades are rigidly connected to each other and mounted on a single teetering (flapping) hinge at the rotor head. When one blade flaps up, the other flaps down. There are no individual flapping or drag hinges, though feathering bearings allow pitch changes.

questions.question: In a fully articulated rotor system, the three hinges provided for each blade are:-

options.text: flapping, feathering, and drag (lead-lag)
flapping, teetering, and pitch
feathering, teetering, and coning
pitch, roll, and yaw

questions.explanation: A fully articulated rotor head provides three hinges per blade: the flapping hinge (allows up/down movement), the feathering hinge/bearing (allows pitch changes), and the drag hinge (allows lead-lag movement in the plane of rotation). This design accommodates all blade movements independently.

questions.question: A rigid (hingeless) rotor system compensates for dissymmetry of lift by:-

options.text: blade flexing rather than mechanical flapping hinges
changing the rotor RPM
varying the tail rotor thrust
using a teetering hinge

questions.explanation: In a rigid (hingeless) rotor system, there are no mechanical flapping or drag hinges. Instead, the blades are designed to flex at their root, allowing them to flap and lead-lag through controlled bending. This blade flexing compensates for dissymmetry of lift in the same way as mechanical hinges.

questions.question: The induced flow through a helicopter rotor disc in the hover is:-

options.text: a downward flow of air accelerated by the rotor blades
an upward flow of air through the disc
a horizontal flow of air across the disc
zero in a stable hover

questions.explanation: In the hover, the rotor blades accelerate air downward through the disc. This downward flow is called the induced flow (or induced velocity). It reduces the effective angle of attack of the blades and is the source of induced drag. The induced flow is relatively uniform across the disc in a stable hover.

questions.question: Induced drag on a helicopter rotor blade is caused by:-

options.text: the tilting of the total aerodynamic force rearward due to the induced flow
the friction of air flowing over the blade surface
the shape of the blade cross-section
the interference between the fuselage and the rotor disc

questions.explanation: Induced drag results from the production of lift. The induced flow (downwash) through the rotor disc tilts the relative airflow downward, which tilts the total aerodynamic force rearward. The rearward component of this force is induced drag. It is greatest in the hover and decreases with forward speed.

questions.question: Profile drag on a rotor blade is the sum of:-

options.text: form drag and skin friction drag
induced drag and parasite drag
wave drag and interference drag
form drag and induced drag

questions.explanation: Profile drag is the drag on the blade due to its passage through the air, regardless of whether it is producing lift. It consists of form drag (due to the shape of the blade cross-section and pressure distribution) and skin friction drag (due to the viscosity of air flowing over the blade surface).

questions.question: The tail rotor is most effective when the helicopter is:-

options.text: hovering with a crosswind from the side that opposes torque
hovering with a tailwind
in fast forward flight
hovering with a crosswind from the tail rotor side

questions.explanation: The tail rotor is most effective when a crosswind blows from the side that assists the tail rotor thrust in opposing torque. This effectively increases the relative airflow through the tail rotor, improving its efficiency. A crosswind from the opposite side can reduce tail rotor effectiveness.

questions.question: Loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE) is most likely to occur during:-

options.text: low speed flight with certain relative wind directions
high speed cruise flight
autorotation at high altitude
hovering in strong headwinds

questions.explanation: Loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE) is most likely during low speed flight (below 30 knots) when certain relative wind directions can interfere with the tail rotor's ability to produce thrust. Main rotor disc vortex interference, tail rotor vortex ring state, and weathercock instability are the three aerodynamic phenomena that can cause LTE.

questions.question: The power required to hover a helicopter is greatest when:-

options.text: hovering out of ground effect at high gross weight and high density altitude
hovering in ground effect at low gross weight
hovering in ground effect at sea level
hovering out of ground effect at low gross weight and low density altitude

questions.explanation: Hover power required increases with: higher gross weight (more thrust needed), higher density altitude (less dense air means higher blade angles and more induced drag), and out of ground effect (no beneficial ground cushion). The combination of all three represents the worst case for hover power.

questions.question: The minimum power speed (bucket speed) in a helicopter is the speed at which:-

options.text: total power required is at its minimum
the helicopter achieves maximum range
induced drag equals zero
the helicopter achieves maximum altitude

questions.explanation: The minimum power speed (also called the bucket speed due to the shape of the power required curve) is the airspeed at which total power required is at its minimum. This is the speed for maximum endurance. It occurs where the sum of induced power (decreasing with speed) and parasite power (increasing with speed) is lowest.

questions.question: The best rate of climb speed (Vy) in a helicopter is the speed at which:-

options.text: the greatest excess of power available over power required exists
the drag is at its minimum
the fuel consumption is lowest
the rotor RPM is highest

questions.explanation: The best rate of climb speed (Vy) is the speed at which the difference between power available and power required is greatest. This maximum excess power can be converted into the greatest rate of climb. It is typically faster than the minimum power speed.

questions.question: The never exceed speed (Vne) of a helicopter is limited primarily by:-

options.text: retreating blade stall and advancing blade compressibility effects
engine power limitations only
tail rotor RPM limits
fuel consumption rate

questions.explanation: Vne is limited by aerodynamic factors: at high forward speeds, the retreating blade must operate at very high angles of attack (risking stall), while the advancing blade tip approaches the speed of sound (risking compressibility effects and shock waves). Both conditions cause severe vibration and loss of control.

questions.question: During a power-off autorotative descent, the rate of descent is controlled by:-

options.text: the airspeed (cyclic control)
the collective lever position only
the anti-torque pedals
the throttle

questions.explanation: During autorotation, the rate of descent is primarily controlled by airspeed, which is controlled by the cyclic. Flying faster or slower than the best autorotation speed increases the rate of descent. The collective is used to control rotor RPM, not the rate of descent (except during the flare and cushion).

questions.question: The height-velocity diagram (dead man's curve) shows combinations of:-

options.text: height and airspeed from which a safe autorotative landing may not be possible
altitude and temperature for safe operations
weight and CG limits
power required and power available

questions.explanation: The height-velocity diagram (H-V diagram or dead man's curve) defines combinations of height above ground and airspeed from which a safe autorotative landing cannot be guaranteed following an engine failure. Pilots should avoid operating in the shaded areas of this diagram whenever possible.

questions.question: The flare during an autorotative landing is used to:-

options.text: reduce the rate of descent and forward speed while increasing rotor RPM
increase the rate of descent
reduce rotor RPM before touchdown
increase forward speed for a running landing

questions.explanation: The flare (aft cyclic application) near the ground during autorotation serves three purposes: it reduces the rate of descent, reduces forward groundspeed, and increases rotor RPM (by converting forward speed energy into rotor energy). The stored rotor energy is then used for the collective cushion just before touchdown.

questions.question: Blade sailing is most likely to occur:-

options.text: during rotor start-up or shutdown in strong or gusty winds
during high-speed forward flight
during autorotation at high altitude
during hovering in calm conditions

questions.explanation: Blade sailing occurs when the rotor RPM is low (during start-up or shutdown) and the blades do not have sufficient centrifugal force to maintain their position. Strong or gusty winds can cause the blades to flap excessively, potentially striking the tail boom or fuselage. Pilots should position the cyclic into the wind during start-up and shutdown.

questions.question: Dynamic rollover is most likely to occur when:-

options.text: one skid or wheel is fixed on the ground and lateral cyclic is applied
the helicopter is in fast forward flight
the helicopter is at high altitude
the helicopter is in a stable hover

questions.explanation: Dynamic rollover occurs when the helicopter pivots about one skid or wheel that is in contact with the ground. If the roll rate exceeds the critical angle (typically about 5-8°), the pilot may not have enough lateral cyclic authority to stop the roll. It can happen during slope operations, crosswind takeoffs, or if a skid catches on an obstruction.

questions.question: The best way to prevent dynamic rollover is to:-

options.text: ensure smooth, gradual control inputs during takeoff and landing, especially on slopes
always take off and land at maximum power
maintain high rotor RPM at all times
avoid hovering in ground effect

questions.explanation: Preventing dynamic rollover requires smooth, gradual collective and cyclic inputs during takeoff and landing. On slopes, the pilot should lift off smoothly and avoid allowing one skid to remain on the ground while applying lateral cyclic. If a roll starts, the immediate action is to lower the collective.

questions.question: Mast bumping is a hazard associated with:-

options.text: semi-rigid (teetering) rotor systems during low-G or negative-G conditions
fully articulated rotor systems in high-speed flight
rigid rotor systems during autorotation
all rotor types during normal hovering

questions.explanation: Mast bumping occurs in semi-rigid (teetering) rotor systems when the rotor disc tilts excessively relative to the mast. During low-G or negative-G conditions (such as a pushover), the rotor disc can tilt beyond its stop limits, causing the rotor hub to contact (bump) the mast, potentially severing it. This is catastrophic.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the correlator (or governor) in a helicopter engine is to:-

options.text: automatically adjust engine power to maintain rotor RPM when the collective is moved
control the tail rotor pitch
adjust the cyclic trim
prevent overspeeding of the rotor in autorotation

questions.explanation: The correlator (or governor) automatically adjusts engine power (throttle) to maintain a constant rotor RPM when the pilot changes the collective position. When the collective is raised (increasing blade pitch and drag), the correlator increases engine power to prevent RPM from drooping, and vice versa.

questions.question: The freewheeling unit (overrunning clutch) in a helicopter allows:-

options.text: the rotor to continue turning when the engine stops or slows below rotor RPM
the engine to run at a different RPM from the rotor during normal flight
the tail rotor to disconnect from the main rotor
the pilot to adjust the gear ratio between engine and rotor

questions.explanation: The freewheeling unit (overrunning clutch) automatically disconnects the engine from the rotor transmission when the engine RPM drops below the rotor RPM. This is essential for autorotation — it allows the rotor to continue turning freely after an engine failure without being dragged down by the stopped or decelerating engine.

questions.question: Coriolis effect in a rotor system causes a blade to:-

options.text: lead when it flaps up and lag when it flaps down
lag when it flaps up and lead when it flaps down
increase its pitch angle when flapping up
decrease its RPM when flapping down

questions.explanation: Due to conservation of angular momentum, when a blade flaps up, its centre of mass moves closer to the axis of rotation, causing it to accelerate (lead) in the plane of rotation — like a spinning ice skater pulling in their arms. When the blade flaps down, the centre of mass moves outward, causing it to decelerate (lag).

questions.question: The advancing blade in forward flight is the blade that:-

options.text: moves in the same direction as the helicopter's forward movement
moves opposite to the helicopter's forward movement
is at the 12 o'clock position
has the highest pitch angle

questions.explanation: The advancing blade is the blade that moves in the same direction as the helicopter's forward flight. Its relative airspeed is the sum of rotational speed plus the helicopter's forward speed. In a helicopter with anti-clockwise rotating blades (viewed from above), the advancing blade is on the right side.

questions.question: The retreating blade in forward flight compensates for its lower airspeed by:-

options.text: flapping down, which increases its angle of attack
flapping up, which decreases its angle of attack
increasing its rotational speed
reducing its chord length

questions.explanation: The retreating blade has a lower relative airspeed (rotational speed minus forward speed). To maintain equal lift across the disc, it flaps down, which increases the angle of attack by changing the direction of the relative airflow. This automatic compensation through blade flapping is how dissymmetry of lift is resolved.

questions.question: The phase lag in a rotor system means that the maximum blade flapping occurs:-

options.text: approximately 90° after the point of maximum pitch change input
at the same point as the pitch change input
180° after the pitch change input
at a random position depending on wind conditions

questions.explanation: Due to gyroscopic precession, the maximum blade displacement (flapping) occurs approximately 90° after the point where the maximum aerodynamic force is applied. This is why cyclic pitch changes are input 90° before the desired disc tilt position. This 90° phase lag is a fundamental property of gyroscopic systems.

questions.question: Pendular action (pendulosity) in a helicopter refers to:-

options.text: the tendency of the fuselage to swing like a pendulum beneath the rotor disc
the oscillation of the rotor blades
the swinging of the tail boom
the vibration of the engine at certain RPMs

questions.explanation: Pendular action is the tendency of the helicopter fuselage to swing like a pendulum beneath the rotor disc. Since the fuselage is suspended below the rotor by the mast, any abrupt control input or gust can cause the fuselage to oscillate. Smooth control inputs help minimise this effect.

questions.question: A helicopter in forward flight requires less power than in the hover because:-

options.text: the rotor operates more efficiently in forward flight due to reduced induced drag
the engine produces more power at higher airspeeds
parasite drag decreases in forward flight
the tail rotor requires less power in forward flight

questions.explanation: In forward flight, the rotor encounters relatively undisturbed air, which reduces the induced velocity (downwash) through the disc. This significantly reduces induced drag, which is the dominant drag component in the hover. Although parasite drag increases with speed, the reduction in induced drag more than compensates at moderate speeds.

questions.question: The maximum range speed of a helicopter is the speed at which:-

options.text: the ratio of speed to fuel flow is greatest
the power required is at its minimum
the rate of climb is greatest
the rotor RPM is highest

questions.explanation: Maximum range speed is the speed that gives the greatest distance per unit of fuel. On the power required curve, it is found by drawing a tangent line from the origin to the curve. This speed is faster than the minimum power speed (maximum endurance speed) because it optimises the speed-to-fuel-flow ratio.

questions.question: The maximum endurance speed of a helicopter is:-

options.text: the speed at which fuel consumption per unit of time is lowest (minimum power speed)
the speed at which fuel consumption per nautical mile is lowest
the never exceed speed
the speed for best rate of climb

questions.explanation: Maximum endurance speed is the speed at which the helicopter can remain airborne for the longest time on a given amount of fuel. This corresponds to the minimum power speed — the bottom of the power required curve — where fuel consumption per hour is at its lowest.

questions.question: Ground resonance is a hazard that can occur in helicopters with:-

options.text: fully articulated rotor systems equipped with drag hinges
semi-rigid teetering rotor systems only
rigid rotor systems only
any rotor system type equally

questions.explanation: Ground resonance is a self-exciting vibration that can occur in helicopters with fully articulated rotor systems (which have drag hinges). If the blades become unevenly spaced in the plane of rotation (due to a hard landing or uneven ground), the resulting vibration can couple with the helicopter's natural frequency on its landing gear, causing a destructive oscillation.

questions.question: The immediate action to recover from ground resonance is to:-

options.text: lift off immediately if RPM is sufficient, or shut down the engine if RPM is insufficient
apply the rotor brake immediately
increase collective slowly
apply full forward cyclic

questions.explanation: If ground resonance occurs and rotor RPM is in the normal operating range, the pilot should lift off immediately to break the coupling between the rotor and the landing gear. If RPM is too low to lift off (during start-up or shutdown), the engine should be shut down immediately and the rotor brake applied to stop the rotor as quickly as possible.

questions.question: The tip path plane of a rotor is:-

options.text: the imaginary plane described by the tips of the rotor blades as they rotate
the plane of the swash plate
the horizontal plane through the rotor mast
the plane perpendicular to the rotor shaft

questions.explanation: The tip path plane (TPP) is the imaginary flat plane described by the tips of the rotor blades as they rotate. The total rotor thrust acts perpendicular to this plane. When the cyclic is moved, the tip path plane tilts, directing the thrust vector in the desired direction.

questions.question: Total rotor thrust acts:-

options.text: perpendicular to the tip path plane
parallel to the tip path plane
always vertically upward
always along the rotor mast axis

questions.explanation: Total rotor thrust is the resultant of all the aerodynamic forces produced by the rotor blades. It acts perpendicular to the tip path plane (the plane traced by the blade tips). By tilting the tip path plane with cyclic input, the pilot directs the thrust vector to control the helicopter's movement.

questions.question: When hovering, if the pilot moves the cyclic forward, the rotor disc will tilt forward because:-

options.text: the cyclic changes blade pitch cyclically, and gyroscopic precession causes the disc to tilt 90° later
the cyclic directly pushes the rotor mast forward
the collective automatically adjusts
the tail rotor thrust changes

questions.explanation: Moving the cyclic forward changes the blade pitch angle cyclically — increasing pitch on one side and decreasing it on the other. Due to gyroscopic precession, the resulting aerodynamic force takes effect 90° later in the direction of rotation, causing the disc to tilt in the direction the cyclic was moved.

questions.question: The effect of a headwind on a helicopter's hovering performance is:-

options.text: improved performance due to translational lift
degraded performance due to increased drag
no effect on hovering performance
degraded performance due to reduced rotor RPM

questions.explanation: A headwind provides a component of translational lift even while the helicopter is stationary over the ground. The wind flowing through the rotor disc reduces the induced velocity, making the rotor more efficient and reducing the power required to hover. This is why helicopters hover more easily into wind.

questions.question: The stalling angle of a rotor blade is typically:-

options.text: approximately 14° to 16° angle of attack
approximately 2° to 4° angle of attack
approximately 30° to 35° angle of attack
approximately 45° angle of attack

questions.explanation: Most rotor blade aerofoil sections stall at approximately 14° to 16° angle of attack. Beyond this critical angle, the airflow separates from the upper surface of the blade, causing a sudden loss of lift and a large increase in drag. The exact stalling angle depends on the specific aerofoil section used.

questions.question: Blade pitch angle and angle of attack are:-

options.text: different — pitch angle is measured from the rotor disc plane, angle of attack from the relative airflow
the same thing measured differently
both measured from the horizontal
both controlled by the cyclic only

questions.explanation: Blade pitch angle (theta) is the angle between the blade chord line and the plane of rotation (rotor disc plane) — it is set by the pilot via collective and cyclic. Angle of attack (alpha) is the angle between the chord line and the relative airflow. They differ because the induced flow (downwash) changes the direction of the relative airflow.

questions.question: Increasing the rotor RPM while maintaining the same blade pitch angle will:-

options.text: increase rotor thrust because the blade tip speed and dynamic pressure increase
decrease rotor thrust
have no effect on rotor thrust
cause the blades to stall

questions.explanation: Increasing rotor RPM increases the rotational velocity of the blades, which increases the dynamic pressure (½ρV²) acting on each blade section. Since lift is proportional to dynamic pressure, the total rotor thrust increases. However, rotor RPM is normally kept constant in flight by the governor/correlator.

questions.question: The reverse flow region on a rotor disc in forward flight is:-

options.text: the area near the root of the retreating blade where the airflow moves from trailing edge to leading edge
the area at the tip of the advancing blade
the entire retreating blade
the area behind the rotor disc

questions.explanation: The reverse flow region exists near the root of the retreating blade where the helicopter's forward speed exceeds the blade's rotational speed. In this region, the air actually flows from the trailing edge to the leading edge of the blade. This area produces no useful lift and increases in size with forward speed.

questions.question: The effect of increasing altitude on helicopter performance is:-

options.text: reduced performance due to decreased air density and reduced engine power
improved performance due to reduced drag
no change in performance
improved performance due to cooler temperatures

questions.explanation: As altitude increases, air density decreases. This reduces the lift produced by the rotor blades (requiring higher blade angles) and reduces engine power output (less air for combustion). Both effects combine to reduce overall helicopter performance — lower hover ceiling, reduced rate of climb, and reduced payload capacity.

questions.question: The weathercock stability of a helicopter is provided primarily by:-

options.text: the vertical fin and the tail boom acting as a weathervane
the main rotor disc
the landing gear
the engine cowling

questions.explanation: Weathercock stability (directional stability) is the tendency of the helicopter to align itself with the relative airflow, like a weathervane. The vertical fin and tail boom provide a large side area behind the CG, which creates a restoring yaw moment when the helicopter is displaced from its heading.

questions.question: Static stability refers to:-

options.text: the initial tendency of the helicopter to return towards its original position after a disturbance
the helicopter's ability to maintain a constant altitude
the helicopter's resistance to control inputs
the long-term oscillation of the helicopter after a disturbance

questions.explanation: Static stability is the initial tendency of the helicopter after being disturbed from its trimmed condition. Positive static stability means the helicopter initially tends to return towards its original position. Negative static stability means it tends to diverge further. Neutral means it stays in the new position.

questions.question: Dynamic stability refers to:-

options.text: the helicopter's behaviour over time after a disturbance — whether oscillations increase, decrease, or remain constant
the initial reaction to a control input
the stability of the engine RPM
the strength of the airframe structure

questions.explanation: Dynamic stability describes the helicopter's motion over time after a disturbance. Positive dynamic stability means oscillations decrease in amplitude over time (convergent). Negative dynamic stability means oscillations increase (divergent). An aircraft can be statically stable but dynamically unstable if oscillations grow over time.

questions.question: The power required to drive the tail rotor is typically:-

options.text: approximately 10% to 15% of the total engine power
approximately 50% of the total engine power
less than 1% of the total engine power
approximately 30% of the total engine power

questions.explanation: The tail rotor typically consumes approximately 10% to 15% of the total engine power available. This is a significant power drain, which is why some helicopter designs use alternative anti-torque systems such as NOTAR (No Tail Rotor) or fenestron (shrouded tail rotor) to improve efficiency.

questions.question: Compressibility effects on the advancing blade tip are most likely at:-

options.text: high forward speeds and high rotor RPM
low forward speeds in the hover
during autorotation at low altitude
during slow flight in ground effect

questions.explanation: The advancing blade tip speed is the sum of rotational speed and forward speed. At high forward speeds, the tip of the advancing blade can approach the speed of sound, causing compressibility effects (shock waves, increased drag, vibration, and loss of lift). This is one of the factors limiting the helicopter's Vne.

questions.question: The coefficient of lift (CL) of a rotor blade depends primarily on:-

options.text: the angle of attack and the blade's aerofoil shape
the weight of the helicopter only
the rotor RPM only
the outside air temperature only

questions.explanation: The coefficient of lift (CL) is determined by the angle of attack and the shape of the aerofoil section. For a given aerofoil, CL increases approximately linearly with angle of attack up to the stalling angle. The aerofoil shape (camber, thickness, etc.) determines the CL at any given angle of attack.

questions.question: A symmetrical aerofoil section produces zero lift when:-

options.text: the angle of attack is zero
the angle of attack is 4°
the airspeed is zero
the blade is at the stalling angle

questions.explanation: A symmetrical aerofoil has identical upper and lower surfaces. At zero angle of attack, the airflow is identical over both surfaces, producing equal pressure distributions and therefore zero net lift. Lift is only produced when the angle of attack is increased from zero. Many helicopter rotor blades use symmetrical or near-symmetrical aerofoil sections.

questions.question: The downwash from a helicopter rotor in the hover creates a hazard for:-

options.text: loose objects, people, and other aircraft on the ground nearby
only the helicopter itself
aircraft flying above the helicopter
only fixed-wing aircraft

questions.explanation: The rotor downwash in a hover can reach speeds of 60-100 km/h depending on the helicopter size. This can blow loose objects, create a brownout/whiteout in dusty or snowy conditions, be dangerous to people on the ground, and affect other aircraft operating nearby. Pilots must always be aware of the downwash effect.

questions.question: Recirculation of rotor downwash during hovering in confined areas can cause:-

options.text: a loss of lift effectiveness and unpredictable control responses
an increase in lift due to ground effect
improved directional stability
no significant effect on helicopter performance

questions.explanation: When hovering in confined areas (near buildings, trees, or walls), the rotor downwash can recirculate back up through the rotor disc. This disturbed, turbulent air reduces the rotor's efficiency, causes unpredictable control responses, and can lead to a loss of lift. Pilots must exercise extreme caution in confined areas.

questions.question: The relationship between indicated airspeed (IAS) and true airspeed (TAS) at altitude is:-

options.text: TAS is higher than IAS at altitude because air density is lower
TAS is lower than IAS at altitude
TAS and IAS are always equal
TAS is only higher than IAS in a descent

questions.explanation: The airspeed indicator measures dynamic pressure, which depends on air density. At altitude, the air is less dense, so the helicopter must fly faster (higher TAS) to produce the same dynamic pressure reading (IAS). The rule of thumb is TAS increases by approximately 2% per 1000 ft above sea level.

questions.question: The primary advantage of a NOTAR (No Tail Rotor) anti-torque system is:-

options.text: improved safety by eliminating the exposed tail rotor blades
increased maximum forward speed
reduced fuel consumption in cruise flight
improved autorotation performance

questions.explanation: The NOTAR system uses a fan-driven air jet through the tail boom and a direct jet thruster at the tail to provide anti-torque. Its primary advantage is improved safety — there are no exposed tail rotor blades that can strike objects, people, or the ground. It also produces less noise than a conventional tail rotor.
